frases.estructura: Question word + verb + subject: in questions the verb comes before the subject, just like in English «How have you…?».
nota: «Hvordan har du det?» is a fixed expression. In English we use «to be» («are»), but Danish uses **har** («have»).
Notice the order: in questions the verb goes before the subject: **har du** («have you»).
analisis: object with no meaning of its own (in the expression «have det»)

frases.estudio: Jeg har det godt, tak. Hvad med dig?
frases.literal: I have it well, thanks. What with you?
frases.estructura: Subject + verb + det + adverb: «have det godt» means «to be well» / «to feel good».
nota: To say that you are well, use the same expression: **jeg har det godt**.
«Hvad med dig?» is the most common way to return the question: «and you?».

texto:
The most useful word in Danish is **hej**: it means «hi», and you can use it at any time of day and with anyone.

To say goodbye you can say **farvel** (goodbye), **hej hej** (more informal) or **vi ses** (see you).

In Denmark almost everyone uses the informal form, so in these lessons we will always use **du** (you).

Next to each word you will see an approximate pronunciation designed for English speakers. It is not exact: it is a help to get you started.

- The syllable in CAPITALS is the stressed one.
- The Danish h is a soft aspirated h, like the h in English «hello».
- Many written letters are not pronounced: «hv» sounds like «v», and the final «t» of «godt» is silent; its «d» is pronounced very softly.

In English we say «I have», «you have», «he has». In Danish the verb is the same for all persons: **jeg har**, **du har**…

On the other hand, the subject is required: you can't just say «har det godt», you have to say **jeg har det godt**.

There isn't one single word for «please» in every context. In a short everyday request, **tak** is usually added at the end:

- **En kaffe, tak.** = A coffee, please.

In notices and formal requests, **venligst** («please») is also used.

opciones.explicacion: «Tak» means «thanks». And if you want to be more polite: «mange tak», thank you very much.
«Hi» is «hej». «Tak» is what you say when someone gives you something.
«Goodbye» is «farvel».
It's a logical mix-up, because «tak» sometimes takes the place of English «please» («En kaffe, tak»). But its meaning is «thanks».

«Tak» means «thanks».
That's «how are you?», a question to start a conversation, not to end it.
«Ja» means «yes».
Literally it is «how have you it?», but it means «how are you?».
To ask someone's name, a different verb is used. We'll see it in lesson 2.
Good catch that «har» means «have», but the expression «have det» + «godt» is about how you are, not what you have.
There is no place word here. «Hvordan» means «how».

pregunta.texto: Choose the Danish sentence that means «I'm fine, thanks».

opciones.explicacion: Remember: in Danish it is said with «har» (have), not with «er» (am/is).
A very typical mistake for English speakers: thinking «I am fine» and using «er». But this expression uses «har» (have).
«Du» means «you». So you would say «you are fine, thanks».
The words are right, but the order isn't: «det» goes before «godt».
«Hvordan har du det?»: the expression uses the verb «at have» (to have).
«Er» means «am/is/are», and in English we would say «are». But this fixed expression uses «har» (have).
«Med» means «with». Here a verb is missing.
«Tak» means «thanks». Here a verb is missing.
«Hvad med dig?» = «and you?». Literally, «what with you?».
«Og» means «and», and it's tempting because in English we say «and you?». But «Hvad og dig?» is not said.
With «har» it would make no sense: «what do you have, you?».
«Tak» means «thanks». Here you need a word that means «with».
